summary: The note explains kerogen, the solid insoluble organic matter in sedimentary rocks formed from compressed and heated dead plants, algae and microorganisms. It describes how kerogen forms during diagenesis and thermal maturation, yielding bitumen, oil and gas, and how its composition, microstructure and physical properties change with maturity. It also classifies kerogen into Types I to IV and notes kerogen-like material found in meteorites and on Mars.
one_line: Kerogen is insoluble fossilized organic matter in sedimentary rocks that generates oil and gas as it matures under heat and pressure.
key_facts: Kerogen is solid, insoluble organic matter in sedimentary rocks made of compressed and heated dead plants, algae and other microorganisms.
All the kerogen on earth is estimated to contain 10 tons of carbon, making it the most abundant source of organic compounds on earth, exceeding living matter 10,000-fold.
The name "kerogen" was introduced by the Scottish organic chemist Alexander Crum Brown in 1906, derived from the Greek for "wax birth".
Kerogen is insoluble in normal organic solvents and has no specific chemical formula.
The soluble portion of kerogen is known as bitumen.
The oil window is about 50–150 °C and the gas window about 150–200 °C, depending on how quickly the source rock is heated.
Kerogen from the Green River Formation oil shale deposit of western North America contains elements in the proportions carbon 215 : hydrogen 330 : oxygen 12 : nitrogen 5 : sulfur 1.
Skeletal density of kerogen increases from approximately 1.1 g/ml at low thermal maturity to 1.7 g/ml at high thermal maturity.
Analysis by gas sorption showed the internal specific surface area of kerogen increases by an order of magnitude (~40 to 400 m/g) during thermal maturation.
Type I kerogen is derived principally from lacustrine algae and has a hydrogen:carbon atomic ratio above 1.25.
Type II kerogen is principally derived from marine plankton and algae and produces a mixture of oil and gas under heating.
Type III kerogen is derived from terrestrial plant matter, has a hydrogen:carbon atomic ratio below 1, and tends to produce gas under heating.
Type IV kerogen comprises mostly inert polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and has no potential to produce hydrocarbons.

Alfred E. Treibs, father of organic geochemistry, extracted a vanadium porphyrin compound from petroleum whose structure closely resembles chlorophyll a, helping establish that petroleum was derived from plants.
The Curiosity rover has detected organic deposits similar to kerogen in mudstone samples in Gale Crater on Mars.
